rows.answer:
The loss to you would be zero. Under the RBI's 2017 circular, if the unauthorised transaction is a third-party breach (the deficiency lies neither with you nor the bank) and you report it within three working days of receiving the bank's communication, you have zero liability. Your report within two days falls inside that window. The bank must also credit (shadow reversal) the amount to your account within 10 working days of your notification, without waiting for any insurance claim settlement.

One caveat: if the breach was actually caused by the bank's own contributory fraud, negligence, or deficiency, you also have zero liability, regardless of when you report. However, if your own negligence were involved, such as sharing payment credentials, you would bear the loss until you report it.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly applies the reference's third-party breach rule: zero liability if the customer notifies within three working days of the bank's communication, and the user's two-day report falls within that window. It also correctly notes that bank-side deficiency gives zero liability regardless of timing, and that customer negligence leaves the customer bearing the loss.

rows.answer: A BSBD account holder can lose at most ₹5,000 per transaction in this case. A report five working days after the bank's communication falls in the 4–7 working day window. There, the customer's liability is the transaction value or the Table 1 amount, whichever is lower. For BSBD accounts the Table 1 maximum is ₹5,000, so a smaller transaction would cap the loss at its own value.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies that a five-working-day delay falls in the 4–7 day window, where per-transaction liability is the lower of transaction value or the Table 1 cap, and that the BSBD cap is ₹5,000.

rows.answer: The customer would be liable for at most Rs 25,000 per transaction, or the transaction value if that is lower. Reporting six working days after the alert falls in the 4–7 working day window, where liability is capped at the lower of the transaction value or the Table 1 amount. A credit card with a limit above Rs 5 lakh falls in the Rs 25,000 category.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly places a six-working-day delay in the 4–7 day window, applies the Rs 25,000 cap for credit cards with limits above Rs 5 lakh, and correctly limits liability to the lower of the transaction value or that cap.

rows.answer: The bank must credit the amount involved (a "shadow reversal") to the customer's account within 10 working days of the customer's notification. It must do this without waiting for any insurance claim to settle. The credit is value-dated to the date of the unauthorised transaction.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states the 10 working days deadline from customer notification, the shadow reversal, no waiting for insurance settlement, and value dating to the unauthorised transaction date, all matching the reference.

rows.answer: A bank must resolve the complaint and establish any customer liability within the time set in its Board-approved policy, and that time cannot exceed 90 days from the date it receives the complaint. If the bank cannot resolve the complaint or determine liability within 90 days, it must still pay the customer the compensation prescribed in paragraphs 6 to 9 of the circular.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the 90-day outer limit from receipt of complaint, the Board-approved policy timeline capped at that, and the compensation obligation if the complaint cannot be resolved within 90 days, matching the reference.

rows.answer: The bank has to prove it. Under paragraph 12 of the RBI's 2017 circular on limiting customer liability, the burden of proving customer liability in unauthorised electronic banking transactions lies on the bank, not the customer.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that the bank bears the burden of proving customer liability in unauthorised electronic banking transactions, matching paragraph 12 of the reference text.

rows.answer: Under the RBI's 2017 circular, sharing payment credentials such as an OTP counts as customer negligence. In that case you bear the entire loss until you report the unauthorised transaction to the bank. Any loss after you report it is borne by the bank, so report immediately and ask the bank to block further transactions. The excerpts don't cover other situations, such as a bank deficiency, which could change the outcome.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that sharing payment credentials such as an OTP is negligence, so the customer bears the entire loss until reporting, with the bank bearing loss after reporting, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Working days are counted according to the working schedule of the customer's home branch, and the date on which the customer receives the bank's communication is excluded from the count. The count is used to place the report in a liability band: within 3 working days means zero liability, 4 to 7 working days means limited liability, and beyond 7 working days is governed by the bank's Board-approved policy.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states that working days follow the home branch's working schedule and exclude the date of receiving the communication, and correctly summarizes the Table 2 bands (within 3 days zero liability, 4-7 days limited liability, beyond 7 per Board policy).

rows.answer: Yes, in part. Under the RBI's 2017 circular, banks may decline to offer electronic transaction facilities to customers who don't provide a mobile number. The exception is ATM cash withdrawals, which banks may not withhold on this basis. The mobile number matters because SMS alerts are mandatory for electronic banking transactions.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states banks may decline electronic transactions (other than ATM cash withdrawals) for customers without mobile numbers, matching the reference; the "2017 circular" attribution is unverified but does not contradict the reference text.

rows.answer: Banks must ask customers to mandatorily register for SMS alerts, and also for e-mail alerts wherever that facility is available. SMS alerts must always be sent to customers, while e-mail alerts may be sent wherever the customer has registered for them.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states that banks must ask customers to mandatorily register for SMS alerts and register for e-mail alerts wherever available, matching the reference text's key requirement.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI's 2017 circular, banks must make sure that, for a debit card or bank account, you do not lose interest while the complaint is being resolved. The bank must resolve the complaint and establish any customer liability within the timeframe in its Board-approved policy, which cannot exceed 90 days. If it cannot do so within 90 days, it must pay you the compensation prescribed in paragraphs 6 to 9 of the circular.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly says no interest loss for debit card/bank account holders during resolution, and accurately states the 90-day cap, Board-approved timeline, and compensation under paragraphs 6 to 9 if unresolved; the "2017 circular" attribution is extra detail not contradicted by the reference.

rows.answer: If the deficiency lies neither with you nor the bank (a third-party breach) and you report it beyond seven working days of receiving the bank's communication, your liability is determined by the bank's Board-approved policy. There is no fixed RBI cap in that case. Banks must disclose this policy when you open an account, display it publicly, and individually inform existing customers. Working days are counted by your home branch's schedule, excluding the day you received the communication.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that for third-party breaches reported beyond seven working days, liability is as per the bank's Board-approved policy with no fixed RBI cap, and accurately covers disclosure, public display, individual notification, and the working-day counting rule.

rows.answer: The Standing Committee on Customer Service in each bank periodically reviews the unauthorised electronic banking transactions reported by customers or otherwise. It also reviews the action taken, and the functioning of the grievance redress mechanism, and takes measures to improve systems and procedures. In addition, the bank's internal auditors must review all such transactions.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies the Standing Committee on Customer Service as the committee that periodically reviews unauthorised electronic banking transactions reported by customers, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI circular on limiting customer liability (2017), a customer has zero liability where the unauthorised transaction results from contributory fraud, negligence or deficiency on the part of the bank. This applies irrespective of whether or not the customer reports the transaction. The three-working-day reporting condition applies only to third-party breaches, where the deficiency lies neither with the bank nor with the customer.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that zero liability applies for bank-side negligence/deficiency irrespective of whether the customer reports the transaction, and that the three-working-day condition applies only to third-party breaches; it answers "No" accurately.

rows.answer: The minimum cooling-off period is one day. The Board of the regulated entity (RE) sets the actual period in its loan policy, and it cannot be shorter than one day. During this period the borrower may exit the loan by repaying the principal and the proportionate APR without penalty. The RE may keep a reasonable one-time processing fee if it disclosed that fee upfront in the KFS.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states the minimum cooling-off period is one day, set by the RE's Board in the loan policy, and accurately summarizes the exit terms and processing fee disclosure condition.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a regulated entity's digital lending app (and any app run by its lending service provider) must not access mobile phone resources such as files and media, the contact list, call logs, or telephony functions. Data collection must be need-based and based on your prior, explicit consent with an audit trail. The only exception is one-time access to the camera, microphone, location, or similar facility, and only for onboarding/KYC, with your explicit consent.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly says no, that DLAs must desist from accessing contact list, call logs, files, and telephony functions, and accurately describes the one-time KYC exception with explicit consent and need-based collection, matching the reference.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a regulated entity must disburse the loan into the borrower's own bank account, and it cannot disburse into any third-party account, including the LSP's. The only exceptions are disbursals required by statute or regulation, fund flows between regulated entities in co-lending, and disbursals for a specific end use. In that last case the money must go directly into the end-beneficiary's bank account.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly says no, disbursal must go to the borrower's account, not to any third-party account including the LSP, and accurately lists the three exceptions (statutory/regulatory mandate, co-lending flows, specific end use with direct payment to end-beneficiary) matching the reference.

rows.answer: If data is processed outside India, it must be deleted from the overseas servers and brought back to India within 24 hours of processing. This is in addition to the general rule that all data be stored only on servers located in India, subject to statutory and regulatory obligations (RBI Digital Lending Directions 2025, para 13(iv)).
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states the 24-hour deadline for deleting overseas data and bringing it back to India, matching reference para 13(iv).

rows.answer: Yes, but only a limited one. If you exit during the cooling-off period, you pay the principal and the proportionate APR without any penalty. The lender (RE) may retain a reasonable one-time processing fee, and if it applies, it must be disclosed to you upfront in the Key Fact Statement (KFS). The cooling-off period is set by the RE's Board in its loan policy and can't be shorter than one day.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states that the lender may retain a reasonable one-time processing fee on cooling-off exit, that it must be disclosed upfront in the KFS, that the borrower pays principal and proportionate APR without penalty, and that the period is set by the Board and is at least one day.

rows.answer: Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), you can escalate if the lender (the regulated entity) has not replied within 30 days of receiving your complaint. You can also escalate sooner if the lender rejects your complaint wholly or partly, or if you are unsatisfied with its reply. You can file through the Complaint Management System (CMS) portal under the RB-IOS, or send a physical complaint to the Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre in Chandigarh.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states the 30-day threshold for no reply from the RE, notes earlier escalation is possible on rejection or dissatisfaction, and accurately names the CMS portal under RB-IOS and the Chandigarh physical complaint option.

rows.answer: The total DLG cover on a loan portfolio may not exceed 5% of the amount disbursed from that portfolio at any given time. For implicit guarantee arrangements, the DLG provider also cannot bear performance risk above the equivalent of 5% of the underlying loan portfolio. The cover is calculated on the amount actually disbursed, so it activates proportionately as loans are disbursed from the fixed DLG set.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the 5% cap on total disbursed amount from the portfolio at any time, and correctly includes the implicit guarantee equivalent of 5% of the underlying portfolio, matching the reference.

rows.answer: A Regulated Entity must invoke a DLG within a maximum overdue period of 120 days, unless the borrower makes good the loan dues before that (Para 26(i) of the RBI Digital Lending Directions, 2025).
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the 120-day maximum overdue period for invoking DLG and the exception if the borrower makes good the dues before that, matching the reference Para 26(i).

rows.answer:
Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a Regulated Entity may accept a Default Loss Guarantee (DLG) only in one or more of these forms:
- Cash deposited with the RE
- A Fixed Deposit with a Scheduled Commercial Bank, with a lien marked in favour of the RE
- A Bank Guarantee in favour of the RE

The total DLG cover on a portfolio is also capped at 5% of the amount disbursed from that portfolio.
rows.judge_reason: The answer lists exactly the three permitted forms in the reference (cash deposited with the RE, fixed deposit with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with lien in favour of the RE, and bank guarantee in favour of the RE). Its extra 5% portfolio cap is not in the provided reference text, but it does not contradict it and does not affect the answer to the question asked.

rows.answer: No. Under para 20(i) of the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a Regulated Entity (RE) may not enter into DLG arrangements for credit cards, as defined in the Master Direction on Credit Card and Debit Card issuance and conduct (2022). The same restriction applies to revolving credit facilities offered through digital lending channels.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that under para 20(i) REs cannot enter into DLG arrangements for credit cards (as defined in the 2022 Credit Card and Debit Card Master Direction) or for revolving credit facilities via digital lending, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a regulated entity (RE) may enter into a DLG arrangement only with a Lending Service Provider (LSP) or with another RE that is engaged as an LSP. An LSP that provides a DLG must be incorporated as a company under the Companies Act, 2013.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states that only an LSP or another RE engaged as an LSP may provide DLG, and that the LSP must be incorporated as a company under the Companies Act, 2013, matching the reference text.

rows.answer:
Yes. Under para 6 of the RBI Digital Lending Directions, 2025, when an LSP has agreements with multiple regulated entities (REs), it must show a digital view of all loan offers that match the borrower's request on the DLA. The names of unmatched lenders must also be disclosed.

Each offer must show the lender's name, loan amount and tenor, APR, monthly repayment obligation, and penal charges (if applicable), so you can compare offers fairly. Each offer must also link to its KFS. The content must be unbiased and must not push a particular lender, including through dark patterns. However, ranking offers by a publicly pre-disclosed metric is allowed.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states that the LSP must show a digital view of all matching offers, disclose unmatched lenders' names, include the required fields (lender name, amount, tenor, APR, monthly repayment, penal charges), provide KFS links, and remain unbiased with the ranking exception.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a regulated entity (RE) must ensure there is no automatic increase in your credit limit. It can raise the limit only after it receives an explicit request from you, evaluates that request, and keeps it on record.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that no automatic credit limit increase is allowed and that an increase requires an explicit borrower request that is evaluated and kept on record, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), a regulated entity (RE) must collect information on the borrower's economic profile before extending any loan. At a minimum, this means the borrower's age, occupation and income details. The RE must keep this information on record for audit purposes.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the minimum information (age, occupation, income details), the requirement to collect it before extending any loan, and the audit record-keeping obligation, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: The Chief Compliance Officer of the regulated entity (RE), or another official designated by its Board for this purpose, must certify that the DLA data submitted on the CIMS portal is correct. They must also certify that the DLAs comply with all applicable regulatory instructions, including the Directions (para 17(iii)). RBI does not verify or validate the data submitted on CIMS.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies the Chief Compliance Officer or another Board-designated official as the certifying authority under para 17(iii), and accurately notes RBI does not verify the data.

rows.answer: No. The data on DLAs is submitted by the RE on the CIMS portal and published on RBI's website automatically, and RBI does not verify or validate it. The RE is responsible for its correctness and timeliness. REs must also ensure that including a third-party DLA in this reporting is not taken by the DLA or any associated entity as registration, authorization, or endorsement by the Reserve Bank, and is not presented that way in marketing or promotional materials.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly says no, explaining that RBI publishes RE-submitted CIMS data automatically without verifying or validating it, and that inclusion does not imply registration, authorization, or endorsement, matching the reference's key points.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions, 2025, the regulated entity (RE) must ensure that neither it nor its lending service provider (LSP) collects or stores biometric data, unless existing statutory guidelines allow it. The RE remains responsible for the privacy and security of your personal information on an ongoing basis. Separately, LSPs may keep only minimal basic data, such as name, address and contact details, needed for their operations.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the core rule: the RE must ensure neither RE nor LSP collects or stores biometric data unless allowed under statutory guidelines, and it correctly notes the RE's ongoing responsibility and the minimal-data limit for LSPs.

rows.answer: The excerpts don't say. Para 27(i) requires LSPs with DLG arrangements to publish on their websites the total number of portfolios and the amount of each portfolio covered by DLG. The text of para 27(ii), which appears to set how the disclosure is to be made, is cut off after "Disclosure under para (i) above shall be made," so the frequency isn't visible. You would need the full text of para 27(ii) to confirm it.
rows.judge_reason: The reference text in para 27(ii) states the disclosure must be made monthly, no later than seven working days after the month ends, but the answer wrongly claims the text is cut off and the frequency is not visible.

rows.answer: No. EMI programmes on credit cards are governed by Para 6(b)(iii) of the Master Direction on Credit Card and Debit Card – Issuance and Conduct, 2022, so they fall outside the Digital Lending Directions. However, other loan products offered on credit cards that the Master Direction para doesn't cover or envisage are subject to the Digital Lending Directions. Loans offered on debit cards, including debit card EMI programmes, are covered by the Directions.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that credit card EMI programmes are governed by Para 6(b)(iii) of the Credit Card and Debit Card Master Direction and fall outside the Digital Lending Directions, and adds the accurate nuances about other credit card loans and debit card EMI programmes.

rows.answer: Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), when a loan defaults and a recovery agent is assigned, or the assigned agent changes, the regulated entity (RE) must send the borrower the particulars of the authorised recovery agent by email or SMS. This must be done before the agent contacts the borrower for recovery.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the requirement from clause 8(v): the RE must communicate the recovery agent's particulars to the borrower via email/SMS before the agent contacts the borrower, covering both assignment and change of agent.

rows.answer: The lender (the Regulated Entity) pays the LSP's fees. Under the RBI Digital Lending Directions (2025), any fees, charges or reimbursements payable to the LSP must be paid directly by the RE. The LSP cannot charge them to you or collect them from you separately. This also applies to cash recoveries on delinquent loans, where the LSP cannot deduct its fees from the recovery proceeds either directly or indirectly.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that the RE (lender) pays LSP fees directly, the LSP cannot charge or collect them from the borrower separately, and this extends to cash recoveries on delinquent loans, matching clause 9(iv) and 9(v).

rows.answer: Under the RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (2024), a bank must give the person or entity served with the show cause notice a reasonable time of not less than 21 days to respond. The bank must examine the response before declaring the account fraudulent. It must then serve a reasoned order giving its decision.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the key requirement accurately: a reasonable time of not less than 21 days to respond to the SCN, matching the reference text; the additional points about examining the response and issuing a reasoned order are consistent with the framework and do not contradict it.

rows.answer: The Board must review the Fraud Risk Management Policy at least once in three years. It may review it more often if the Board prescribes a shorter interval (Para 2.1.2 of the RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management, 2024).
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states the Board must review the policy at least once every three years and may review more frequently as the Board prescribes, matching paragraph 2.1.2 of the reference.

rows.answer: Banks must set up the Special Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of cases of Frauds (SCBMF). It needs at least three Board members: a whole-time director and at least two independent or non-executive directors. One of the independent or non-executive directors must head the committee.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the SCBMF composition: minimum three Board members, a whole-time director plus at least two independent/non-executive directors, headed by one of the independent/non-executive directors, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Under the Master Directions, the bank must report the red-flagged status on the RBI's CRILC platform immediately, and no later than seven days from the date it classifies the account as red-flagged (Para 4.1.3). The directions do not distinguish large accounts here. Separately, if the account is then classified as fraud, the Fraud Monitoring Report (FMR) must be filed with the RBI within 14 days of that classification (Para 6.3.1).
rows.judge_reason: The answer gives the key requirement accurately: report on CRILC immediately and no later than seven days from the red-flag classification, which matches both 3.3.4 and 4.1.3. The extra 14-day FMR point cites a paragraph not in the reference, but it does not affect the answer to the question asked.

rows.answer: The RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (2024) say the Risk Management Committee of the Board (RMCB) should prescribe an appropriate Turnaround Time (TAT) for examining EWS alerts or triggers. The TAT should preferably be no more than 30 days.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the key requirement accurately: RMCB prescribes an appropriate TAT for examining EWS alerts, preferably not more than 30 days, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Ordinarily, a bank should complete the process of classifying a red-flagged account as fraud, or removing its red-flagged status, within 180 days from the date the account was first reported as red-flagged on the CRILC platform. Cases that remain red-flagged beyond 180 days must be reported to the Special Committee of the Board for Monitoring and Follow-up of Frauds (SCBMF) for review with adequate justification, and they are also subject to RBI supervisory review.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the 180-day ordinary completion period from first CRILC reporting, plus the SCBMF review and RBI supervisory review for cases remaining red-flagged beyond 180 days, matching the reference.

rows.answer: The excerpts don't state the period outright. They only refer to a "mandatory cooling period" in Para 4.4.1, which runs from full payment of the defrauded amount or the amount agreed in a compromise settlement. From my recollection of the 2024 Master Directions, that period is five years, but please check Para 4.4.1 to confirm. Once it ends, lenders have sole discretion to grant or decline credit.
rows.judge_reason: The answer gives the correct five-year period, but wrongly says the excerpts don't state it, hedges it as recollection, and adds unsupported claims (a "mandatory cooling period" label and lenders' "sole discretion" after the period ends) that aren't in Para 4.4.1.

rows.answer: A private sector bank that finds a fraud of ₹2 crore must report it immediately to the State/UT Police. Because the amount is ₹1 crore or above, it must also report to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO), Ministry of Corporate Affairs, with the details submitted in the Fraud Monitoring Return (FMR) format (Para 5.1 of the RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management, 2024).
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly identifies both required agencies for a private bank fraud of ₹1 crore or above (State/UT Police and SFIO, Ministry of Corporate Affairs) and notes the FMR format reporting, matching the reference text.

rows.answer: Under the RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (2024), a public sector bank or regional rural bank must report fraud cases of ₹6 crore and above to the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). Cases below ₹6 crore go to the State/UT Police.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that public sector banks (and RRBs) must lodge complaints with the CBI for fraud amounts of ₹6 crore and above, with below ₹6 crore going to State/UT Police, matching the reference table.

rows.answer: The excerpts don't say how soon a bank must file the Fraud Monitoring Return (FMR) after classifying a fraud. They only explain that the "date of detection" reported in the FMR is the actual date the fraud came to light, not the date of approval. The "date of classification" is the date the competent authority approves the classification and the reasoned order is passed. The only timelines given are different ones: red-flagged accounts should ordinarily be classified as fraud or cleared within 180 days, and theft, burglary, dacoity and robbery must be reported within seven days. For the FMR filing deadline, you would need to check the other parts of the Master Directions.
rows.judge_reason: The reference explicitly states FMR must be furnished immediately but not later than 14 days from the date of classification, yet the answer claims the documents don't specify this timeline and points to other parts of the Master Directions.

rows.answer:
Under the 2024 Master Directions (para 6.4.2), a bank may close a reported fraud case for limited statistical/reporting purposes if the amount involved is up to ₹1 crore and it has examined staff accountability and taken any disciplinary action. In addition, one of two conditions must hold:

- The investigation is still going on, or the LEA has not filed a charge-sheet, for more than three years from the FIR date.
- The charge-sheet has been filed, but the trial has not started or has been pending for more than three years from the FIR date.

Banks must keep details of all such closed cases available for auditors' examination.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the key conditions accurately: amount up to ₹1 crore, staff accountability examined and any disciplinary action taken, and either the investigation/charge-sheet not filed for over three years from FIR, or trial not commenced/pending for over three years. The auditor-examination sentence is not in the quoted reference but does not contradict it.

rows.answer: Banks must subject title deeds and related title documents to periodic legal audit and re-verification for all credit facilities of ₹5 crore and above, until the loan is fully repaid. The threshold is lower, at ₹1 crore, for Small Finance Banks, Local Area Banks and Regional Rural Banks.
rows.judge_reason: The answer states the ₹5 crore threshold for commercial banks along with the continuing-until-fully-repaid condition and the ₹1 crore threshold for SFBs, LABs and RRBs, all matching the reference.

rows.answer: For FMR reporting, the 'date of detection' is the actual date the fraud came to light in the concerned branch, audit or department. It is not the date the bank's competent authority approved the classification (that is the separate 'date of classification') (Para 8.4.2).
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly states that the date of detection is the actual date the fraud came to light in the branch, audit or department, and not the date of competent authority approval, matching Para 8.4.2. The added reference to a separate 'date of classification' is extra detail not in the excerpt but does not contradict it.

rows.answer: Under the Master Directions, a bank must report a robbery, including an attempted one, to the Fraud Monitoring Group (FMG) in RBI's Department of Supervision, Central Office, immediately and no later than seven days from its occurrence. The bank must also include the case in the quarterly Return on theft, burglary, dacoity and robbery (RBR). The RBR is filed on the online portal within 15 days of the end of the quarter.
rows.judge_reason: The answer accurately states the reference requirement: robbery (including attempts) must be reported to the FMG, Department of Supervision, immediately and no later than seven days from occurrence. The extra details about the quarterly RBR return and its 15-day filing deadline are not in the reference text, but they do not contradict it or change the core answer.

rows.answer:
Generally, the **paying (drawee) bank** reports the fraud, not the presenting bank. For forged or fake instruments, including those sent in clearing as truncated instruments, the paying banker reports to law enforcement agencies and RBI. The presenting bank must promptly hand over the underlying instrument when the paying bank asks for it.

The exception is where the instrument is genuine but payment went to someone who isn't the true owner, or where the presenting bank credited the amount before realisation and the instrument was later returned as fake or forged. In those cases the presenting bank, which is defrauded or put to loss, files the fraud report with RBI and informs the LEAs.
rows.judge_reason: The core answer is correct: the paying (drawee) bank reports forged-instrument frauds, including truncated clearing instruments, and the presenting bank must hand over the instrument on demand. However, the added exception, that the presenting bank reports when it credited before realisation and the instrument was later returned as forged, contradicts the reference's rule that such reporting is "not by the presenting banker." The exception is not supported by the reference text.

rows.answer: No. Under the RBI Master Directions on Fraud Risk Management (2024), para 8.2, banks must complete the investigation from the fraud angle before transferring a loan account or credit facility to other lenders or ARCs. If the bank concludes that a fraud has been perpetrated in the account, it must report the fraud to RBI/NABARD before selling the account.
rows.judge_reason: The answer correctly says no, citing para 8.2: investigation from the fraud angle must be completed before transfer to other lenders/ARCs, and any fraud conclusion must be reported to RBI/NABARD before sale, matching the reference.

rows.answer: Public sector banks (PSBs) and AIFIs must refer all fraud cases involving ₹3 crore and above to the Advisory Board for Banking and Financial Frauds (ABBFF), constituted by the CVC. The referral is for examining the role of all levels of officials and whole-time directors, including ex-officials and ex-WTDs. Cases involving very senior executives, such as the MD & CEO or an Executive Director, must also be referred to the ABBFF in PSBs and AIFIs.
rows.judge_reason: The answer gives the key threshold of ₹3 crore and above, matching the reference, and its added point about senior executives is consistent with the reference's coverage of whole-time directors.

rows.answer: Under paragraph 6.3.6, a bank may withdraw an FMR or remove a perpetrator's name from it only in exceptional circumstances. The withdrawal or removal must have due justification and be approved by an official at least in the rank of a whole-time director.

rows.answer: Yes, but only to the former management.
